newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-SAMPRAS OUT-POWERS WOODBRIDGE IN WIMBLEDON SEMI.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS OUT-POWERS WOODBRIDGE IN WIMBLEDON SEMI.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras out-powered doubles champion Todd Woodbridge on Friday, swamping the Australian 6-2 6-1 7-6 in their Wimbledon semifinal.
The three-times former singles champion answered every Woodbridge doubles finesse with a huge serve or a thumping return and the slight Australian found no way through.
"Today I played one of the greatest players who was playing great," Woodbridge, 26, said afterwards.
Sampras produced only 10 aces in the match, fewer than usual, but his serve was still a lethal weapon.
"The way he serves a second ball is what sets him apart from other players," Woodbridge said.
Despite some lovely doubles touches from neat lobs to scorching passing shorts, Woodbridge was broken twice in the first set, twice in the second and once in the third.
"I'm playing very solid. I've been getting better each match," Sampras said.
Woodbridge did manage six break points against Sampras's serve in the match, but the cool American saved all but one.
That one in the fourth game of the first set produced the first break of the Sampras serve since his first round match against Mikael Tillstrom of Sweden 10 days ago.

Woodbridge, who defeated world number two Michael Chang in his first round match, had not beaten Sampras, 25, since their first meeting at Wimbledon in 1989. Sampras, who captured his first of nine Grand Slam tournaments at the U.S. Open at the age of 19, had won their four encounters since.
The American, who beat former three-times champion Boris Becker in the quarter-finals on Thursday, looks unbeatable on grass.
"There's no weakness today that I've noticed that I could have pounced on or used against him," said Woodbridge, who was due to play a doubles semifinal with his partner Mark Woodforde later.
Sampras, who goes on to play either Michael Stich of Germany or Cedric Pioline of France in the final on Sunday, commented: "I'd rather be in the final of Wimbledon than anywhere."
